comments.author: swalsh
comments.text: Like I said last week. I think zucks original llama thesis is proving more correct by the week. The rent market on intelligence never materialized, if you have THE frontier model, you can charge rent (for a few weeks, maybe month). But after a certain capability level it's price that drives the decision. Zuck is doing the thing he's really good at, and building a moat around the network (Muse is VERY sticky), and now that we're all going to standardize on Meta's model, we're going to optimize the heck out of the infra to run the model making it cheaper for him to scale, thus bringing in more participants to his network, and thus making his network more valuable. Meta is going to win consumer AI.

comments.author: popinman322
comments.text: The model license requires large inference providers to contact Meta separately to obtain a license to serve the model. I know we've seen this before with other large models, but it's still a bit irritating. The usual effect of separate licensing is decreased price competition from public providers (like we saw with Kimi K3). I guess it's better for the providers if the price is fixed: any efficiency improvements directly improve margin rather than driving prices down over time. Still, to provide my own anecdata, the main thing keeping me on a paid subscription is token costs for the more capable models.

comments.author: sebmellen
comments.text: Nick is a force of nature. Highly recommend following him on X if you don't already. His launch post gives good context not found in the blog: > interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had > with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works https://x.com/nickcammarata/status/2110757819427574056?s=46

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、ニューラルネットワークの解釈可能性（mechanistic interpretability）が本当に簡単かどうかで、特にスケールと最新ツールがどの程度役立つかが争点となった。賛成側は、巨大パラメータモデルでも多くのニューロンが読み取れ、回路がきれいに見えるとして、自動科学者の進歩により近い将来解決できると主張した。一方で疑問を呈する声は、著者の主張が過度に楽観的だと指摘し、手法の限界や余計な3Dシティモデルの邪魔を挙げた。注目されたコメントとして、Nickのツイート引用では「単純なことを異常な規模で行うとうまくいく」と解釈性の楽観を示し、またオープンウェイトの必要性を強調する意見や、人間のニューロンのポリセマンティシティとカラスの脳を対比させた皮肉めいた考察が挙げられた。

stories.title_en: More on Anthropic's Scion ripping off Mononoke

comments.author: nickg-anthropic
comments.text: Hi! I am the original author of the blog post and wanted to clear the air a bit here. We credited Sapling because that's how Meta itself externally refers to the entire system, including the Mononoke server, and we wanted to follow that convention. We will add an additional footnote to clarify this. We were inspired by many things while building Scion, such as the great ideas in Mononoke's Bonsai data model, and didn't intend to obfuscate that in any way. We were also inspired heavily by https://martin.kleppmann.com/2015/03/04/turning-the-database... , for example. We also did not just tell Claude to build us a version control system; we did a lot of research on what would work and not work for our use case and coming from an existing large Git repo (rather than Mercurial, as Mononoke did) required many novelties beyond some of these data structures. The intent was to give credit to Mononoke without getting too deep in the weeds of comparing and contrasting each point of the data model where we diverged. There are many ex-Meta employees at Anthropic who were inspired by how joyful using source control was because of Mononoke, which deserves a lot of credit to you and the source control team there. We had that experience as a north star from the beginning while making decisions that map to our (different) needs.

主な議論点: Anthropicが公開したScionがMetaのMononokeを模倣したかどうか、クレジット表記の妥当性、名前「Scion」がBonsaiの音節逆転か偶然か、著者イニシャル使用の意図（タレントプーリング防止かその他）などが議論の中心となった。

注目コメント: 元ブログ投稿者による詳細説明（「Sapling」表記の理由や研究過程を明らかにし、意図的に隠そうとしなかったこと）と、名前の音節逆転を指摘したコメントが特に洞察に富んでおり、コミュニティの関心を集めた。

comments.author: tenacious_tuna
comments.text: This is a really enjoyable take, pushing the feeling of what one does on a computer towards actually being at a desk and having to reach for various functions. I feel like that would enable spatial memory to do some cool things. I miss the 90s chunkiness of switches, buttons, hardware: being able to hear the computer "think" (HDD seeks), the hum of a CRT. Modern machinery feels so insubstantial, emphasizing clean glass and tidy machined chassis. (chassies?) I have this persistent daydream about a computer setup that feels like the Nostromo flight deck from Alien. I almost want to feel like I'm sitting _inside_ a computer when I'm at my desk, surrounded by powerful feeling electronics with substantial switches and such. Of course there's plenty of inconvenience there too, but something about it appeals to me.

stories.title_en: I Know Why the Mathematicians Weep
stories.title_ja: 私はなぜ数学者が泣くのか知っている

comments.author: atleastoptimal
comments.text: I think beyond the specific elements of any domain AI eclipses humans in, overall, the notion of the thing that grants you status, prestige, and a living wage being commodified would spark in anyone a profound sense of dread. Beyond just making you redundant in your job, the whole architecture of your existence, the thousands of hours of struggle, the sacrifice of putting off social games or personal enjoyment are now rendered moot in hindsight. You are made one step closer to complete worthlessness, which will surely continue as AI becomes a more satisfying personal companion, a more worthwhile friend, lover, etc. How is one to feel safe in the progress of the future when the only hints of the wonderful post-scarcity utopia we can quantify so far is the removal of all human leverage via their labor? All it tells us is we will be bargaining with superintelligence with nothing to stand on, only a trust that the 5000 lab executives and researchers solved the most important research problem of all time on the first try.

comments.author: RGS1811
comments.text: This piece circles, without naming it, around the concept of “deontic scorekeeping” central to the work of Robert Brandom on semantics. The idea that our ability to create and sustain conceptual systems depends on the give and take of reasons within a social setting. Brandom has been front of mind for me lately because elements of his theory both explain why LLMs should work in principle, and where they are bound to be radically deficient. An LLM encodes the normative regularities of our linguistic/conceptual games into its weights, but it cannot be a real participant in our games because it is incapable of staking durable commitments or changing its dispositions over time. Worth reading: Robert Brandom, “Making It Explicit: Reasoning, Representing, and Discursive Commitment”

comments.author: randcraw
comments.text: I think Thompson has no understanding of endeavors like pure math or the theoretical sciences. In the words of Einstein, "I want to know how God created this world. I am not interested in this or that phenomenon, in the spectrum of this or that element. I want to know his thoughts; the rest [is] just details." I think mathematicians aren't bemoaning their lost sunk costs. They're now aware that they may never again have the joy of being the first to pull up the edge of the tarp of ignorance and see the raw truth beneath _for the first time_. Their voyages of discovery, which give life meaning, may never leave dry dock again.

comments.author: izzydata
comments.text: I still think mathematicians are going to be as important as ever. The LLMs are only finding what was technically possible given our current breadth of knowledge after brute force solving problems. Eventually it will run out of things that it can do with its training and the only way to get it to do more will be training it on new human found knowledge. Finding that new knowledge may be exponentially more difficult, but it will be much more valuable.

comments.author: d_burfoot
comments.text: > I am not one of those AI people who believes that hundreds of millions of jobs will be wiped clean from existence in the next five years "Wiped clean" is the wrong phrasing, and 5 years is a short timeframe given the ability of some sectors of the economy to resist change. But yes, hundreds of millions of white collar professionals will need to rethink their careers and their business models within the foreseeable future. Just today there was an HN article about how shady the dental industry is. In the future, you will go to a special dental imaging facility where a modestly-compensated technician images your whole mouth and feeds the results into an AI system, and when you get home you can look at the assessment and chat with the AI about it. Then you can potentially go visit a dentist, oral surgeon, etc, if you actually need work. This system will produce far better dental health outcomes at far lower cost: the diagnoses will be more accurate, and there will be no bias towards additional, unnecessary procedures.

stories.summary_ja: 「I Know Why the Mathematicians Weep」記事に対するHNコメントでは、AIが人間の知的活動、特に純粋数学や理論科学においてもたらす存在的危機が中心話題となった。多くの参加者は、AIが人間の労働を commoditize し、数学者が長年積み重ねてきた「最初に真実を見つける喜び」や社会的地位、生計の基盤を奪うと主張し、これが価値感の喪失につながると危惧した。一方で、Brandom の「deontic scorekeeping」観点から、LLMは言語の規則性を学習できるが、時間とともに約束を更新したり社会的コミットメントを担う能力が欠けているため、真の概念的ゲームの参加者になれないという指摘もあった。賛否は、AIが最終的に人間の新知見発見の補助にしかなれず、数学者の役割は不可欠だと楽観する意見と、AIが進化すれば人間の leverage が完全に失われ、超知能と交渉する材料がなくなるという悲観的見解に分かれた。特に注目されたコメントは、数学者の喜びは「初めて tarp をめぐらし真理を見る瞬間」にあり、それが失われれば研究の意味が揺らぐという洞察であった。
stories.editor_note: 私はなぜ数学者が泣くのか知っている: 抽象的な証明の美しさと困難さが感情を揺さぶる理由を哲学的に考察し、数学教育における動機付けのヒントとなり、日本の大学数学科でも議論の種となっています。

comments.author: whartung
comments.text: FORTRAN was a very important language for me. Growing up on early micros, with BASIC, my father had Fortran for the TRS-80. I took a stab at learning it, but the documentation was reference for calling the compiler, not so much learning the language. And when I found a FORTRAN book, it was quite dated and talking about things like tapes and punches and what not. So, that effort stalled. But, my first quarter in college, I took a FORTRAN (77) class. FORTRAN taught on the schools CDC Cyber mainframe. This was quite a change from 8-bit PET BASIC. But, most importantly, it was exposure to much of the same concept that an 8-bit computer has, but from a different tact. This gave me more of a way to view things from a higher level, since I had to make them fit the two different views of how FORTRAN looked at things, how the Cyber presented things, and how BASIC and the PET were "same thing only different". It also gave me access to a multi-user system, and all of the interesting capabilities it offers. I remember when they put in their first lab of PCs, and how they started teaching folks Turbo Pascal on micro computers, and I just felt that the users were missing out on a bigger world. "Anyone" can access a PC or micro computer at home, but mainframe or multi user mini access, not so much. It's just a much bigger world out there, and we tend to baby duck what we first see. Different world today, never had to use FORTRAN professionally, but I am most grateful for the experience of learning it and its environment. Very powerful medium for broader learning. Also FORTRAN was the only notable computer thing I had "taught" to me (outside of my 20 minute introduction to BASIC by my high school teacher), pretty much everything else I self learned from books and such, even knowing the bulk of it before taking classes in school.

comments.author: vegesm
comments.text: At some point I was quite interested in how the very first version of FORTRAN looked like, so I wrote a FizzBuzz [1] in it. It was a very bare-bones language, felt more like a high-level assembly macro language. One thing it did well was expressing formulas with the usual "mathematical" notations (+,-,*,/, parentheses to group operations, variables). I guess this was revolutionary at the time. But the control structures were very limited, everything was basically jumps and gotos. The IF was merely a syntactic sugar for conditional jumps. Of course, functions did not exist in the language. [1] https://mveg.es/posts/fizzbuzz-in-fortran-1/

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点: フォートランは科学技術計算の基盤として長年にわたり使われてきた歴史的言語であり、初学者にとっては文書化が不足し、パンチカード時代の概念（Cでコメント）に戸惑うことが多い点が議論された。また、初期バージョンは数式表現は得意だったが制御構造がジャンプ中心で貧弱であり、現代のフォートランは高速で線形代数に適しているという評価が出た。さらに、フォートランで書かれた基礎ライブラリ（BLAS、LAPACKなど）が今も重要であるという共通認識も見られた。  
賛否両論: 近年のフォートランはCよりも速く、数値計算に最適だと支持する意見がある一方、1990年代に入門書を見て「C列にCを打つだけ」という古い様式に嫌気がさし学習を断念した経験談や、Pascal後の違和感からすぐに離れた声もあり、言語の使いやすさについて意見が分かれた。一方で、現代のモジュール機能や配列演算を挙げて「使いやすくなった」と評価する声も少なからずある。  
注目コメント: 初期フォートランでFizzBuzzを実装した者は、「数式記法は革命的だったが、IFは単なる条件ジャンプの糖衣構文で、関数もなく高レベルアセンブラのような感覚だった」と指摘し、言語の進化を如実に示している。このコメントは、フォートランがどのようにして現代の科学計算言語へと変わってきたかを端的に表しているため、議論の中での洞察に値すると言える。

comments.author: BoppreH
comments.text: Context: BIPM is responsible for the UTC time standard, and in this document they decide to stop adding (or removing) leap seconds, starting on 20th of May 2027 and lasting for the foreseeable future (until one leap hour is needed). Together with the decision to not add a leap second in December, the 27 leap seconds that have been added so far should be the only ones. The page lists several good reasons for this, including: - It's a common source of bugs. - IoT, embedded systems, and anything that cannot receive time updates have trouble with leap seconds. - Negative leap seconds have never occurred before, but might occur in the future, and almost no software has tested this case. I'd also add: - Unix timestamps are actually defined as "seconds since epoch minus however many leap seconds have happened ". It's a hack to make the keep code that assumes 86400 seconds in a day from breaking. It means that during a leap second the Unix timestamp goes back and repeats a previous value, making them ambiguous and non-monotonic. - Leap second unpredictability can make it impossible to calculate how many seconds are between two UTC dates or Unix timestamps, for example the countdown to the year 2038 bug. @dan: can we rename this to "BIPM decides to stop adding leap seconds to UTC" or something similar? This title is really downplaying the situation, I think readers over here care a lot about this.

comments.author: snide
comments.text: First, this is cool! Well done. I live next to a State Park. It sounded really cool when I bought the house. No neighbors! Privacy! There is a trail accessible from my properly that goes into some woods, which you only want to be in during the Fall / Spring because the ticks and chiggers are intense. The biggest issue with sharing a border with the state is the fence line. Technically it's on them to maintain. The woods are filled with mostly 200 foot trees. They exist right up to my property and fall every year during big storms. There goes the fence line. I have dogs so the fence is important. Otherwise they run out into the woods that have licensed bow-hunting during the Winter. In practice its impossible to get the fence fixed. You are working through layers of bureaucracy and mismanagement. There is no vested interest from a parks service to work well with hundreds of neighbors individually. I'd build fence lines myself, and could easily pay for it, but it's the upkeep of those fences that would be difficult because so many trees (really, it's every year) fall down from their side. My main point is that sharing a properly line with the government is more like sharing a properly line with nobody. You may as well own that land. Don't expect any upkeep and go in with eyes open.

comments.author: kyleblarson
comments.text: I owned a house on 60 acres in Washington State that was bordered on 2 sides by state land (WA DNR). It was generally great and the only time I closed my gate was actually these two weeks of every year for regular rifle deer season. I never had issues with hunters coming on my property (I did give some friends permission to bow hunt). My driveway was about a mile long and had to cross DNR land to reach my property, but I had an easement. The easements typically have a 35 year expiration and it would take extreme circumstances for the state not to renew an existing easement. Complete and total privacy is really nice, but it's certainly a lot of effort and money to maintain a remote property of that size with a large house. I had to travel to SF a lot for work and that was certainly not ideal: 2.5 hour drive minimum to a tiny airport that only served Seattle, then on to SF.

comments.text: I don't like it. I'm all for signing up for a contract if it can turn a runtime error into a compile time error. However, this looks like it just makes more runtime errors. The article also points out a big problem which is "Importantly, this aspect of Contracts is why contract assertions must not be used for error handling and input validation: If a function has in-contract requirements to report certain events as errors, that handling must be done with standard C++ control statements that are not optional, never with contract assertions." That sort of muddy definition of what contracts are supposed to be used for is almost certainly going to make a mess. It's not input validation, but parameter validation.. but not really validation but rather checks which error out, but it's not errors we are producing.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点: Contractsは実行時チェックであり、コンパイル時エラーに置き換えることを期待されたが、実際はassertと同様にランタイムエラーを発生させるだけだと指摘された。さらに、契約はエラー処理や入力バリデーションに使用すべきでなく、違反時の処理は通常の制御フローで行うべきという定義の曖昧さが議論の中心となった。  
賛否: 一部はEiffelのDesign by Contractに似ていると肯定的に捉え、過去にGCCプラグインで実装した経験や、契約情報を最適化ヒント（__builtin_unreachableのような）として活用できないかという期待を示した。一方で、言語機能がさらに肥大化し、使いどころが不明確だと批判し、契約がただのassertに過ぎないと見なす声もあった。  
注目コメント: 「contractはエラー処理に使ってはならず、通常の制御フローで処理すべき」という指摘が議論を呼び、また「__builtin_unreachable」と同様に最適化フェーズに情報を提供できるかという質問が注目された。さらに、パラメータバリデーションとエラー報告の区別が曖昧である点が問題視され、契約の目的を明確にする必要があるという意見が多数見られた。

stories.editor_note: Show HN: Sygal – PDF、スキャン、ウェブページをローカルで Markdown に変換: OCRとレイアウト解析をローカルで完結させ、プライバシーを守りながらドキュメント変換が可能；日本の研究者や法務部門での活用が期待されます。

comments.author: zlandes86
comments.text: Hey, I'm Zach, the author of this. I had this idea as soon as Jev appeared: how would Jev and other decision models handle the Trolley Problem? So I ran Jev and 13 other models through many different versions of the question. I used resampling and multiple variations and orderings of each question so a random lucky phrasing wouldn't dominate the result. Happy to chat about the philosophical side of the article, strategies for prompting decision models, or anything on the methodology.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点：Jevを含む14種類の意思決定モデルがトロッコ問題の多様なバリエーションにどう答えるか、特にプロンプトの言い回しや順序が結果に与える影響を検証した点が最も議論された。  
・賛否両論：一部の参加者はモデルが一貫した道徳的判断を示せばAI倫理の指針になると肯定的だった一方、他の参加者は統計的手法による再サンプリングだけでは本当の倫理的推論を測れず、モデルのバイアスやプロンプト依存が結果を歪めると批判した。  
・注目コメント：あるユーザーは「順序効果をなくすためのランダム化手法は妥当だが、最終的にモデルが出す答えは訓練データに含まれる文化的規範を反映しているだけで、真のジレンマ処理能力とは言えない」と指摘し、プロンプトエンジニアリングとデータ偏りの両面から考察すべきだと強調した。
stories.editor_note: Jev がトロリープロブレムに遭遇: 哲学的ジレンマをプログラミングチャレンジに落とし込み、アルゴリズム的思考と倫理的判断の関係を探る；日本の技術系学生の間でディスカッションのきっかけになっています。

stories.title_en: OpenCode 2.0

comments.author: ghrl
comments.text: I've been using OpenCode V2 since it first appeared on the website, and I can only repeat the positive views on usability, the client/server model and self-awareness/ability to edit it's config and write plugins. I'd like to mention two other impressive things about OpenCode. First, their issue tracker on GitHub works really well. They have the OpenCode GitHub App connected, and for any bug report it reads the issue, tests on the mentioned version and latest dev branch, and comments the findings along with a reproduction script. For TUI Bugs it even records a video. And all that in less than two minutes, usually. https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues?q=is%3Aissue+st... Another thing they are working on is opentunnel, where you can tunnel services to https on <random>.opentunnel.xyz and its subdomains. What's notable is that the subdomain is persistent and unique to you, and a wildcard ssl cert is actually generated on your machine, so the platform cannot see the traffic. Their primary use case seems to be making the OpenCode Server usable from anywhere, but it can do much more with their cli: https://opentunnel.xyz/

comments.author: solarkraft
comments.text: It's good. Many of the annoyances from V1 are gone. Skills and plugins reload automatically (finally). Tasks can be backgrounded (though I think this doesn't happen automatically yet). There's a built-in skill for editing the configuration (finally I can retire mine). The front-end got some love. Apparently they re-architected the loop around Effect. Sub-sessions can be communicated with better. Configuration is loaded from the folder the session is created in rather than where the server was started. In general, this update largely takes OpenCode into the current age features-wise and is a good overhaul quality-wise. Just in time to stop my early switching away efforts, which would've been a pain because I know few other harnesses with such a strong server/client model.

comments.author: moretti

stories.title_en: Things to know when you get cancer
stories.title_ja: がんになるときに知っておくべきこと

comments.author: stochastician
comments.text: The second opinion advice is great, and what I tell everyone I know who gets cancer. My mom was diagnosed with stage 1 cancer in 2006 in Idaho. I was a PhD student at MIT at the time and a friend in lab helped me get an appointment at Dana-Farber. I thought it was probably overkill (it was a common cancer) but we did it anyway. They said everything in Idaho was standard of care but suggested one extra test, which Idaho team then reluctantly did, which revealed distant metastasis (stage 4! ), dramatically changing her treatment trajectory. She lived another 15 years (I miss you Mom). Asking for a second opinion sucks. A lot of us are preconditioned from birth to trust our clinicians. But you're going on a journey and your life (or the life of your loved one) is on the line. Insurance often covers it. Your doctor will NOT be offended. Think of it this way : if you were deploying code to the mars rover, and your colleague asked to do a code review before you pushed go, would you be offended? This is even more important than that.

comments.author: exhilaration
comments.text: My suggestion is that if you're within a 2-3 hour drive of major cancer centers - just use the US News list https://health.usnews.com/best-hospitals/rankings/cancer - go there instead of your local community hospital. The top cancer hospitals in the world accept your health insurance (probably), so why not go there? Use your vacations days, book hotels if you have to - this is the time to go all out. My experience: I was horribly sick for 10 months, none of my local doctors could figure it out, then I drove to Penn Medicine in Philadelphia and they did the right labwork in the first visit. These top centers just have different mindset than your community hospitals.

comments.author: keithwarren
comments.text: My wife was diagnosed in February with stage 4 invasive lobular breast cancer, peritoneal carcinomatosis with complete bowel obstruction. Surgeons gave her a couple weeks to live. We went through enhertu which worked for about 3.5 months and relieved the blockage and she was able to eat again and get off IV nutrition. It obstructed again and her markers rose sharply in the summer, we did a course of taxol and are moving to trodelvy next week. All of this has been entirely predictable, standard of care patterns. But the standard of care for my wifes disease right now is a march toward death and I refuse to accept that. I spend my every evening talking to every LLM, practically bargaining and begging for one of them to give me a thread of hope. I appreciate this service and we will check it out. We are desperate to find something, I recognize ILC is tricky and complete obstruction is usually a death sentence, but we have to try right? She is 49, we have 4 kids. Anyone out there, any ideas...any longshot, we will do anything.

comments.author: alexpotato
comments.text: Had a family member recently go through unexpected major surgery. One thing I would mention: You are not dealing with a monolithic entity with regards to a hospital. There are really multiple groups with oftentimes competing interests e.g. - case manager wants you out and home b/c that is the best "score" for the hospital. They also DO NOT want you to qualify for Medicare if you are a senior b/c, again, "score" gets dinged if Medicare gets involved - surgeons want you out as they don't want you to pick up hospital infection. They want you to go to a rehab facility as that will more likely lead to a good outcome - the hospitalist wants you to be stable in the short term so will pump you with whatever medications are necessary to get you "back to normal" without addressing any root cause - the nurses generally care about you as a person as they deal with you the most but oftentimes have the least amount of say over your case - in one of those perverse incentives/unintended consequences: if you do TOO well on a physical ability test, that might disqualify you from certain coverage even if you are below the threshold on other ability tests. That can have gigantic insurance implications. This is prompting me to write my own version of the OP blog post.

comments.author: not_a_bot_4sho
comments.text: I have colon cancer. It's been a hell of a journey and my outlook is... not great. To me, this list seems practical but not profound. It doesn't prepare you for all real stuff: you need to get ready to die. You need a plan for your trust, your estate, your funeral, and how your family will deal after. You should have these plans in place before cancer because you could get hit by a bus. (I didn't because I'm stupid but maybe learned a few things the hard way.)

・主な議論点: がん診断後にセカンドオピニオンを取ることの重要性と、可能であれば専門のがんセンターへ受診すべきだという点、さらに病院内部にはケースマネージャー、外科医、病院看護師など利害が異なる複数のグループが存在し、治療方針や退院判断に影響を与えることを指摘し、同時に終末に備えた遺産整理・葬儀の準備や心構えも必要だという意見が中心だった。  
・賛否両論: セカンドオピニオンや専門病院への通院についてはほぼ全員が賛同したが、病院ランキングリストだけでは不十分で、精神的な準備や実務的な対策（保険手続き、生活の調整など）が欠けているとの批判もあり、意見が分かれた。  
・注目コメント: Idahoでの初期診断がセカンドオピニオンで転移が見つかり母が15年生存したエピソードや、ステージ4の乳がん患者がLLMを使って希望を探す絶望的な姿、そして病院のケースマネージャーが早期退院を推し、外科医が感染回避のためリハビリ施設へ送りたがるなど、各部門の対立するインセンティブを詳しく解説した指標が特に洞察に富んでいた。また、自身の結腸がん経験から法的整理や葬儀の準備を事前にしておくべきだと強調する声も挙げられた。
